[00:00] Laura: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Laura from Redwood, AE on the account, and Carlos our SE will go deep on Private VPC networking and runtime impacts.
[00:14] Maya: Hi Laura, hi Carlos. We have a few folks on the call, I'll try to interrupt if network diagrams are needed. We're mainly focused on private deployment — low latency for inference and strict egress control.
[00:25] Carlos: Great, thanks Maya. Quick agenda: networking patterns we see (PrivateLink vs NAT/egress), ENI and subnet sizing, DNS and split-horizon, then runtime impacts — KV cache, batching, quantization, and recommended benchmark steps.
[00:40] Tom: Quick security note — we need to ensure we can meet Azure/AWS cross-account KMS access patterns, and audit logs. SOC2 proof will be needed later.
[00:52] Laura: We'll share the security pack after this call. Carlos, over to you.

--- Technical deep dive ---
[01:05] Carlos: Ok, starting with PrivateLink: we usually recommend PrivateLink when you want inbound access to the Redwood control plane or model registry without transiting the public internet. PrivateLink creates an interface endpoint (ENI) in the customer's VPC that connects to Redwood's service in our account. The benefit is zero public egress and it simplifies ACLs.
[01:30] Maya: Are there throughput or ENI limits we need to worry about? Our VPC has pretty strict ENI caps per subnet.
[01:42] Carlos: Good call. Each interface endpoint uses an ENI; bandwidth is per-AZ, and AWS enforces ENI quotas per instance type/region. For high-throughput inference, we recommend adding multiple endpoints across subnets/AZs and leveraging cross-AZ routing. Also ensure your subnet sizes allow additional ENIs — we provide a template to estimate needed IPs.
[01:59] Lina: If we do PrivateLink, how does data plane traffic flow for inference? We want model payloads to stay within our VPC and not go through Redwood's public endpoints.
[02:10] Carlos: For PrivateLink with Redwood Private, control plane calls (model versioning, health checks) go over the interface endpoint. The inference data plane can be deployed as a customer-managed lambda of our runtime inside the VPC (in the Private deployment pattern), or we can place the runtime in your VPC as a dedicated service — in both cases model traffic stays on your network. There's also an option for mirrored endpoints: a VPC peer or Transit Gateway setup if you prefer.
[02:34] Maya: We use Transit Gateway heavily; is that compatible?
[02:38] Carlos: Yes, Transit Gateway and TGW attachments are compatible — you just need route propagation for the subnets where runtime nodes live. Watch out for propagation limits and route table entries though.

[02:55] Tom: If we can't do PrivateLink initially, what's the recommended egress pattern? We prefer no direct internet.
[03:02] Carlos: Two common patterns: NAT egress through controlled NAT Gateways with firewall rules and proxy, or use a VPC endpoint service. With NAT you must account for SNAT port exhaustion at high-concurrency scenarios. We generally advise — for high token-per-second workloads — prefer PrivateLink because NAT SNAT scaling can become an operational headache (ports, ephemeral port reuse).
[03:26] Maya: Did you say SNAT port exhaustion? Can you quantify?
[03:30] Carlos: Roughly, each ephemeral connection uses a source port; with many concurrent connections from many workers you can hit ~65k ports per NAT IP. If you have 1000 workers each making many short-lived TLS connections per inference batch you can hit limits. We provide a calculator for expected egress ports per workload.

[03:50] Carlos: Next, DNS. Split-horizon DNS is important. If you use PrivateLink or internal endpoints, ensure the private hosted zone/conditional forwarding points to the VPC endpoints so the runtime resolves the internal addresses. Misconfigured DNS will make nodes try public addresses, which breaks private connectivity.
[04:10] Lina: We run CoreDNS on EKS — will Redwood's sample config work?
[04:14] Carlos: Yes, we have sample CoreDNS stanzas and /etc/resolv.conf guidance. We'll include the exact entries in the repo link — https://redwood.ai/docs/private-vpc (note: placeholder) — that show the conditional forwarders.

[04:30] Carlos: Now runtime impacts. KV cache — we sometimes see it transcribed as K-V cash — sorry, K-V cache — is critical for reducing repeated compute. However, cache hits are local to a node unless you deploy a shared cache layer. If your request routing can bounce across nodes you may see more cache misses which raises latency.
[04:53] Maya: So affinity is important?
[04:56] Carlos: Yes. Session affinity (sticky routing) or a shared redis-backed KV cache can help. We typically recommend per-node KV cache with sticky routing for low-latency real-time inference, and shared cache for large scale horizontal workloads with more complex consistency tradeoffs.
[05:12] Lina: What's the latency penalty for a KV cache miss?
[05:15] Carlos: On a cache miss for a long context (e.g., 4k tokens) you'll need to re-populate past KV which can add tens to low hundreds of milliseconds depending on batch sizes and model. The runtime uses optimized streaming build paths so it's not linear but it's noticeable.

[05:36] Carlos: Batching tradeoffs: batching increases throughput but also adds queuing latency. For synchronous low-latency SLAs we recommend small per-request batching with adaptive batch windows (we can configure a max wait of e.g., 10ms to collect requests). For high-throughput background jobs, larger batch sizes with larger latency SLOs are fine. We showed a chart — I'll attach it after the call.
[05:58] Maya: Do you support dynamic batching tuning?
[06:01] Carlos: Yes, the runtime supports adaptive batching and can be constrained by max latency or max batch size. There's also CPU/GPU kernel selection for quantized models which changes optimal batch sizes.

[06:15] Carlos: Quantization — 4-bit vs 8-bit — gives better throughput but some delta on quality. For embeddings and retrieval-heavy workloads we often quantize aggressively; for sensitive generative outputs we tune on eval sets. Quantization also changes memory footprint which impacts how many replicas you can run on a node and thus affects ENI/IP planning.
[06:40] Lina: Any tips for evaluating quality impact quickly?
[06:43] Carlos: Use a small eval prompt set and Redwood's eval harness. We can run side-by-side with your prompts. Also we have rollback profiles — can serve a quantized variant and fall back to full-precision for specific routes.

[07:00] Maya: Let's talk telemetry and benchmarks — what telemetry should we expose?
[07:05] Carlos: For benchmarking: per-route latency p50/p95/p99, token/sec, KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and socket-level metrics (retransmits, TLS handshake time). We recommend exposing these to your observability stack; we can send a Grafana dashboard template.

[07:24] Carlos: On the networking side for benchmarks: ensure subnet MTU is consistent, and disable flow logs or sample them — high-volume flow logging can add noise. Also ensure your firewall isn't doing deep packet inspection that re-handshakes TLS — that would blow up latency.

[07:45] Tom: About KMS/HSM integration — can Redwood sign requests, or do we need to expose keys?
[07:51] Laura: For Private we support customer-managed keys via your KMS. Our control plane has a way to integrate in a cross-account pattern: we never ask for persistent key material. For HSM-backed keys we have a partner integration; we'll include the integration notes in the security pack.

[08:08] Carlos: A few gotchas we see in enterprise deployments:
- IP exhaustion in small subnets when autoscaling nodes come up quickly.
- Misconfigured route tables so runtime tries AZ-local endpoints that don't exist.
- DNS TTLs causing stale SRV records during failover.
- SNAT port exhaustion if using NAT for many concurrent TLS connections.

[08:35] Maya: For the pilot we plan ~10 nodes, 4 GPUs each, and target 4k tokens/sec sustained, p95 latency under 300ms. Is that in scope for Private with PrivateLink?

[08:50] Carlos: Yes, that's reasonable. For p95 300ms you'll want per-node KV cache hit rates >80% or sticky routing, and batch sizes tuned to keep per-token GPU latency low. We'll provide a pilot runbook. Our SE team can run a gold-standard benchmark with your prompt set.

[09:10] Lina: One more question on cross-account VPC peering vs PrivateLink — if we want to connect multiple account-owned VPCs, what's recommended?
[09:18] Carlos: For multi-account, Transit Gateway or PrivateLink endpoint services are both viable. PrivateLink scales better for controlling access per account (you can expose an endpoint service and accept principals). TGW is good if you already have a hub-and-spoke architecture. Choose based on your existing infra and routing limits.

[09:38] Tom: Any special consideration for on-prem and air-gapped?
[09:42] Carlos: For air-gapped we provide an on-prem bundle where the control plane is in your network. You'd run an appliance or containerized control plane; network-wise it's similar but you need to ensure the runtime can reach model stores (S3-like or local object store). We'll provide the checklist for storage, DNS, and internal registry access.

[10:05] Carlos: I'll also outline the flow for TLS certs — we support customer-provided certs and automatic rotation via ACME if you prefer. Cert management ties into your key rotation policy.

[10:20] Maya: Sounds good. Can you repeat the immediate deliverables?
[10:23] Laura: Sure — Carlos will send the network diagram and NAT vs PrivateLink recommendation with templates. I'll send SOC2/KMS/HSM docs. Maya will send CIDRs and current route tables. We'll schedule the benchmark pilot next week.

[10:40] Lina: Quick transcribe issue: you mentioned KV cache population streaming — can you share exact numbers for expected extra latency for a 4k context when cache miss occurs?
[10:48] Carlos: Rough numbers: initial population can add 80–250ms depending on batch and model; streaming build is faster if you use prefix caching. We'll include microbenchmarks in the runbook.

[11:05] Tom: For audit logs — we need API-level access logs shipped to our SIEM. Do you support pushing logs to S3 or CloudWatch?
[11:12] Laura: Yes, we can forward audit logs to your S3 bucket (cross-account role) or to CloudWatch where you can aggregate into your SIEM. We'll include config steps.

[11:28] Carlos: Wrapping up — A couple of notes: prefer PrivateLink if you want minimal operational overhead and strict no-internet policy; NAT is possible but requires careful SNAT planning; persist sticky routing to maximize KV cache effectiveness; use adaptive batching with a small max-wait for low-latency routes; quantify quantization with an eval set and use rollout policies for safe production.

[11:55] Laura: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.

[12:00] Maya: Thanks — appreciate the clear guidance.
